1.note: The pronoun **they** refers to messengers whom King Josiah **sent** out. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the king sent out messengers who gathered to him]

2.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:3. Alternate translation: [And the king went]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:18. Alternate translation: [to the temple of Yahweh]

The author is saying **every** and **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and people from throughout Judah and the various parts of Jerusalem]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and every man and woman of Judah]

The author is providing a further description of the crowd of people from **Judah** and **Jerusalem** who gathered at the temple. By naming two extremes, **small** and **great** (poor and rich, or ordinary and powerful, or young and old), he means those extremes and everything in between. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [including people from a wide range of ages and classes]
See how you translated the similar expression in 18:26. Alternate translation: [in their hearing]

The expression **having been found** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that Hilkiah had found]

3.note: The author says in 11:14 that it was a “custom” for a new king to stand “by the pillar,” apparently a certain one of the pillars on the temple porch, as a visible sign of his loyalty to Yahweh. Josiah had already been the king for 18 years, but he was now symbolizing that he and his people were making a new start by together pledging their loyalty to Yahweh. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And the king stood by the pillar to show that he and his people were making a new start]
See how you translated the similar expression in 11:4. Alternate translation: [and he made a covenant]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:14. Alternate translation: [in the presence of Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:18. Alternate translation: [to live as Yahweh wished]

The terms **commandments**, **testimonies**, and **statutes** mean similar things. The author is using the three terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [all of his commandments]

The author is referring to all of a person by naming two major components of a person, his **heart** and his **soul**. These represent overlapping aspects of the inner life of a person, representing a person’s thoughts, feelings, desires, and intentions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Kings 2:4. Alternate translation: [wholeheartedly] or [with his entire being]

The author is speaking as if the **words of this covenant** were objects that Josiah could **raise up**. He means that Josiah pledged to make happen what the covenant said should happen. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Kings 2:4. Alternate translation: [to make happen what the covenant said] or [to bring the covenant back into effect]

The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that that scroll recorded]

The author is using **stood in the covenant** as a common expression of his culture to mean “agreed to the covenant” or “became parties to the covenant.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all of the people joined in the covenant] or [And all of the people agreed to the terms of the covenant]

4.note: The expression **having been made** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that previous kings had made] or [that previous kings had commanded their workers to make]
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:16. Alternate translation: [and for all the lights in the sky] or [and for the heavenly bodies]

Bringing the **ashes** of the burned idolatrous objects to the city of **Bethel**, which was outside the borders of Judah but under Judean control, was a symbolic action by which Josiah showed that he wanted no trace of these objects to remain in his kingdom. Furthermore, since idolatry in Israel had begun when Jeroboam placed a calf image in Bethel, this was a symbolic way of sending idolatry back to where it began in order to end it definitively. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he sent their ashes out of Judah to Bethel, where Israel’s idolatry had begun]

5.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [to the sun and to the moon and to the constellations, yes, to the whole army of the heavens]

6.note: Since any contact with a dead body, including walking over a grave, made a person ceremonially unclean (Numbers 19:16), throwing the **dust** of the **Asherah** pole that had been in the temple onto a **grave** was a symbolic action by which Josiah rendered the remains of this object unclean and completely unsuitable for use in worship. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he threw its dust over the grave of the sons of the people to make it defiled]

In this verse, the word **grave** is singular in form, but it refers to all of the graves in this area outside Jerusalem. It appears that people who could not afford a tomb cut into rock were buried in a common plot there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “grave.” Alternate translation: [the graves of]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:16. Alternate translation: [the common people]

7.q: אֲשֶׁ֣ר הַ⁠נָּשִׁ֗ים אֹרְג֥וֹת שָׁ֛ם בָּתִּ֖ים לָ⁠אֲשֵׁרָֽה
7.note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. You can do the same with the similar expression in the next verse. Alternate translation: [where women were weaving houses for Asherah]

7.q: אֲשֶׁ֣ר הַ⁠נָּשִׁ֗ים אֹרְג֥וֹת שָׁ֛ם בָּתִּ֖ים לָ⁠אֲשֵׁרָֽה
7.note: Since actual **houses** are not something that people make by **weaving**, the author seems to be using the term to represent something else. Interpreters are not entirely sure what this was, but many suggest that these were either fabric coverings for images of Asherah or small, decorated tents representing dwellings for Asherah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could suggest one of these meanings in your translation. You could also use a general expression. Alternate translation: [where women wove coverings for Asherah images] or [where women did weaving for Asherah]

8.note: The author is referring to all of the territory of Judah by naming two extremes, the city of Geba at its northern edge and the city of Beersheba in the far south. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout the territory of Judah]

The author is using the expression **high places** to represent the kind of shrines that people built on high places, that is, on hilltops. Since these were in cities, at their **gates**, they would not necessarily have been in the highest location in a given area. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the gate shrines]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the gate**, he means the main gate of Jerusalem. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [at the main gate of the city]

9.q: אַ֗ךְ לֹ֤א יַֽעֲלוּ֙ כֹּהֲנֵ֣י הַ⁠בָּמ֔וֹת אֶל־מִזְבַּ֥ח יְהוָ֖ה בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם כִּ֛י אִם־אָכְל֥וּ מַצּ֖וֹת בְּ⁠ת֥וֹךְ אֲחֵי⁠הֶֽם
9.note: The author is providing background information about the priests he described in the previous verse. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

9.q: לֹ֤א יַֽעֲלוּ֙ כֹּהֲנֵ֣י הַ⁠בָּמ֔וֹת אֶל־מִזְבַּ֥ח יְהוָ֖ה בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם
9.note: Not allowing the **priests** who had previously served at the **high places** was a symbolic action by which Josiah kept any trace of false worship away from the Jerusalem temple. These priests were descendants of Aaron who had been burning incense to Yahweh, but they had been doing so at unauthorized locations. This worship was therefore impure, and those who had led the people in it had to be kept away from Yahweh’s altar. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote.

The author is using **go up to the altar** as a common expression of his culture to mean “offer sacrifices on the altar.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [serve at the altar of Yahweh] or [offer sacrifices on the altar of Yahweh]

The author is using one kind of food that the priests received as their share of sacrifices, the **unleavened bread** that they made from grain offerings, to mean all of the food that the priests received from sacrifices for their support. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [However, they were allowed to live off the food from the priests’ share of the sacrifices]

The author is speaking as if the other priests were actually the **brothers** of these priests who had been serving at hilltop shrines. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [together with their fellow priests]

10.q: לְ⁠בִלְתִּ֗י לְ⁠הַעֲבִ֨יר אִ֜ישׁ אֶת־בְּנ֧⁠וֹ וְ⁠אֶת־בִּתּ֛⁠וֹ בָּ⁠אֵ֖שׁ לַ⁠מֹּֽלֶךְ
10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 16:3. Alternate translation: [so that no one could burn up his son or his daughter completely as an offering to Molech]

11.note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can use an expression that would be natural. Alternate translation: [And he burned up the chariots of the sun]

12.note: This could mean: (1) that these **altars** were on the **roof** of an **upper chamber** that **Ahaz** had built somewhere in the palace complex. Alternate translation: [that were on the roof of the upper chamber of Ahaz] or (2) that these **altars** were on the **roof** of the palace, near an **upper chamber** that **Ahaz** had built. Alternate translation: [that were on the palace roof near the upper chamber of Ahaz]

12.q: וַ⁠יָּ֣רָץ מִ⁠שָּׁ֔ם וְ⁠הִשְׁלִ֥יךְ אֶת־עֲפָרָ֖⁠ם אֶל־נַ֥חַל קִדְרֽוֹן
12.note: The verbs **ran** and **threw** together express a single idea. The word **ran** tells in what way Josiah removed the dust and **threw** it into the Kidron Valley (or had his servants do this). If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And he hastened to have their dust thrown into the Valley of Kidron]

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 4:12. Alternate translation: [that were in front of Jerusalem] or [that were opposite Jerusalem]

The author is speaking of directions in the way characteristic of his culture, in which people described directions as if a person were facing east, toward the sunrise. The south would be to the right of such a person. So the author means these **high places** were on the south side of the mountain. Alternate translation: [that were on the south side of]
See the discussion of this name in the introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [the Mount of Olives]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:12. Alternate translation: [the Ammonites]

14.note: Since contact with a dead body caused ritual uncleanness, putting human bones on the sites of these high places made them unsuitable for any further use in worship. See how you explained the significance of Josiah’s similar action of scattering the dust of the vessels of Baal and Asherah on human graves in 23:6.

16.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [according to the message from Yahweh]

16.q: אֲשֶׁ֤ר קָרָא֙ אִ֣ישׁ הָ⁠אֱלֹהִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר קָרָ֔א אֶת־הַ⁠דְּבָרִ֖ים הָ⁠אֵֽלֶּה
16.note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [about these things that the man of God had proclaimed]

17.note: The men of the city are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [That monument is the grave of the man of God]

18.note: Josiah is using two phrases to say basically the same thing, first positively and then negatively. The repetition emphasizes the idea that the phrases convey. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Let no one disturb his bones at all]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [So the men of the city rescued his bones]

To translate the name **Samaria**, meaning the northern kingdom of Israel, here and in the next verse, see how you decided to represent it in 17:24. Alternate translation: [the prophet who was from the northern kingdom]

19.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 5:18. Alternate translation: [the shrines on high places]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **provoking anger**, he means that the **kings of Israel** provoked Yahweh’s anger when they made these shrines. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [provoking Yahweh’s anger]

20.note: The author does not mean that Josiah **sacrificed** these **priests** to Yahweh. He did not offer them on these **altars** as human sacrifices. Rather, he means that Josiah slaughtered them right on their pagan altars as if they had been sacrifices. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And he slaughtered]

21.note: The expression **written** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [as this scroll of the covenant specifies]

22.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand the significance of what Josiah did in this instance. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **had not been done** contains a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one had observed the Passover in this way]
See how you translated the similar expression in 10:36. Alternate translation: [from the time of the judges]

The author is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [the Israelite judges]

23.q: כִּ֗י אִם־בִּ⁠שְׁמֹנֶ֤ה עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה לַ⁠מֶּ֖לֶךְ יֹֽאשִׁיָּ֑הוּ נַעֲשָׂ֞ה הַ⁠פֶּ֧סַח הַ⁠זֶּ֛ה לַ⁠יהוָ֖ה בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
23.note: If it would appear in your language that the author was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement, combining verses 22 and 23. Alternate translation: [The only occasion on which the Israelites celebrated Passover during the whole time that the judges judged Israel and kings ruled in Israel and Judah was in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, when the people of Jerusalem observed Passover for Yahweh]

The expression **was done** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the people observed this Passover]

24.note: See how you translated these expressions in 21:6.

The term **teraphim** describes idols that people in this culture kept in their homes. If your readers would not be familiar with what these were, in your translation you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a general expression. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 15:23. Alternate translation: [and the household idols]

The author is using the term **seen** in a way characteristic of his language and culture to mean that these **abominations** could be seen, that is, they were present in **Judah** and **Jerusalem**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the comparable expression “that was found” in 20:13. Alternate translation: [that were]
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:3. Alternate translation: [in order to bring back into effect]
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:3. Alternate translation: [that the scroll recorded]

25.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 17:2. Alternate translation: [before him]
See how you translated the similar expression in 23:3. Alternate translation: [energetically with his entire being]

The author is speaking as if a later king might have physically **arisen**, or gone up into the air or to an elevated location. In contexts such as this, this expression describes a person assuming a powerful position. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Kings 14:7. Alternate translation: [one like him has not come to power] or [one like him has not reigned]

26.q: לֹֽא־שָׁ֣ב יְהוָ֗ה מֵ⁠חֲר֤וֹן אַפּ⁠וֹ֙ הַ⁠גָּד֔וֹל אֲשֶׁר־חָרָ֥ה אַפּ֖⁠וֹ בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֑ה
26.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 13:13. Alternate translation: [Yahweh remained very angry with the anger that he felt against Judah]

26.q: לֹֽא־שָׁ֣ב יְהוָ֗ה מֵ⁠חֲר֤וֹן אַפּ⁠וֹ֙ הַ⁠גָּד֔וֹל אֲשֶׁר־חָרָ֥ה אַפּ֖⁠וֹ בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֑ה
26.note: The author is using a construction in which a verb (**burned**) and its object (**burning**) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, whether or not you retain some or all of the image in your translation, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s anger continued to burn greatly against Judah] or [Yahweh continued to feel very great anger against Judah]

In this instance as well, the author is using a construction in which a verb (**provoked**) and its object (**provocations**) come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [all that things that Manasseh had done that made him angry]

27.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה גַּ֤ם אֶת־יְהוּדָה֙ אָסִיר֙ מֵ⁠עַ֣ל פָּנַ֔⁠י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֲסִרֹ֖תִי אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
27.note: The author seems to be rephrasing what Yahweh said in 21:13, “I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria.” So it would be appropriate to use a verbal form in your language, as the ULT does, that shows that this is something Yahweh had said in the past, not something that he said even after Josiah made all of his reforms.
See how you translated the similar expression in 13:23. Alternate translation: [away from this land]
If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [I said that my name would be there]
See how you translated the similar expression in 21:7. Alternate translation: [It will be a special place for people to worship me]

28.q: וְ⁠יֶ֛תֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י יֹאשִׁיָּ֖הוּ וְ⁠כָל־אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֑ה הֲ⁠לֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יְהוּדָֽה
28.note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is concluding the story of Josiah. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar phrases in 1:18.

29.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:20. Alternate translation: [During his reign]

In this context, the word **meet** has the sense of “oppose.” Josiah was not coming to greet or support Neco but to fight him in order to keep him from marching his army through Judean territory. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to oppose him]
The pronoun **he** refers to Neco, while the pronoun **him** refers to Josiah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but Neco killed Josiah]

In this context, the word **saw** has the sense of “encounter.” Josiah and Neco did not have a face-to-face meeting at or after which Neco killed Josiah. When their armies fought, Josiah was killed in the battle. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when he encountered him]

30.note: Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people such as Josiah’s **servants** or soldiers, who are the subject in the previous sentence. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And he was buried] or [And people buried him]

31.q: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְ⁠שָׁלֹ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ יְהוֹאָחָ֣ז בְּ⁠מָלְכ֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה חֳדָשִׁ֔ים מָלַ֖ךְ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְ⁠שֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔⁠וֹ חֲמוּטַ֥ל בַּֽת־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ מִ⁠לִּבְנָֽה
31.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is introducing **Jehoahaz** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in 8:26.

32.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:2. Alternate translation: [And he did what Yahweh considered to be evil]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [his ancestors]

33.note: See how you decided to represent the weight of a kikkar in 5:5.

34.note: Changing Eliakim’s name was a symbolic action by which Neco asserted his sovereignty over Judah and its ruler. (Since Eliakim means “God will establish” while Jehoiakim means “Yahweh will establish,” it is possible that Neco allowed Eliakim to choose his own new name. The symbolic significance was in the fact that Neco forced him to change his name.) If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he changed his name to Jehoiakim to assert his sovereignty over him]

35.note: Here, **the land** represents the people who lived in the land of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but he assessed the people of the land] or [but he determined how much each person should pay]

Here, Pharoah’s **mouth** represents what he said by using his mouth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the amount of silver that Pharaoh had demanded]

The author is using one thing that Neco had demanded, the **silver**, to mean both things that Neco demanded, the silver and the gold. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the silver and gold]

36.q: בֶּן־עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְ⁠חָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָ֨ה יְהוֹיָקִ֣ים בְּ⁠מָלְכ֔⁠וֹ וְ⁠אַחַ֤ת עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְ⁠שֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔⁠וֹ זבידה בַת־פְּדָיָ֖ה מִן־רוּמָֽה
36.note: In this verse and the next verse, the author is introducing **Jehoiakim** as a participant in the story as the new king of **Judah**. To translate this verse, see how you translated the similar expressions in 8:26.

37.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:2. Alternate translation: [And he did what Yahweh considered to be evil]
